Friends and colleagues also knew him as an energetic host, a tireless traveller and someone whose enthusiasm for sharing food and wine was matched only by his devotion to his family. Matthew Jukes leaves behind an extraordinary legacy. As a writer, broadcaster, buyer and entrepreneur, he helped influence how a generation of consumers thought about wine while maintaining a deep understanding of every part of the trade, from restaurant lists and retail shelves to brand building and production. Tributes from across the wine world are certain to reflect the respect and affection in which he was held. For now, however, the drinks industry is left mourning the loss of one of its brightest and most distinctive voices.

title: E&A Scheer names Mitch Wilson as head of global rum development
summary:
Global rum specialist and supplier E&A Scheer has appointed Mitch Wilson to the newly created role of head of global rum development.

The post E&A Scheer names Mitch Wilson as head of global rum development appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Global rum specialist and supplier E&A Scheer has appointed Mitch Wilson to the newly created role of head of global rum development. Wilson joins E&A Scheer with nearly 15 years of experience in the rum category, including international ambassador roles with Maison Ferrand and Black Tot Rum. Based in Amsterdam, Wilson is set to lead the commercial growth of the group’s single cask programme, support bespoke rum projects and help expand category education as part of E&A Scheer’s commercial team.

Investment

Speaking about the hire, E&A Scheer CEO and chief rum officer Carsten Vlierboom said: “The future of rum lies in quality, authenticity and long-term partnerships. We’re continuing to invest in the premium end of the category and in the expertise that helps our customers succeed. Mitch’s experience complements our technical knowledge and strengthens our ability to help customers create extraordinary products and brands.” Wilson explained: “I’ve spent nearly 15 years exploring every stage of the rum journey, from distilleries and production to hospitality, retail, education and global brand building. Joining E&A Scheer is an opportunity to apply that experience at the source, helping customers make smarter decisions from cask selection and blend development through to the finished product. Together, we can combine unrivalled access to outstanding Rum with commercial insight to help build stronger brands and continue elevating the category.”

Integration

As part of its continued investment in high-end rum, E&A Scheer has revealed that it is also further integrating its internationally recognised single cask rum specialist, The Main Rum Company, into its Amsterdam operations, bringing its expertise and  inventory under one roof. While The Main Rum Company label will continue to serve those sourcing single cask rums, the company has highlighted that the integration creates "a more streamlined destination for high-quality aged stocks and rare single casks".

title: Reasons to celebrate International Beer Day
summary:
The global celebration International Beer Day is held annually on the first Friday of August. db raises a glass to the initiative.

The post Reasons to celebrate International Beer Day appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
The global celebration International Beer Day is held annually on the first Friday of August. db raises a glass to the initiative. International Beer Day (IBD) was founded back in 2007 in Santa Cruz, California and began as a way of bringing people together to enjoy great drinks, thank local staff, and celebrate global brewing traditions. August was chosen for its summer weather and distance from other beer celebrations, and the event spans more than 200 cities globally. Now, brewers and beer venues are using the date to springboard their own campaigns and marketing activities. Examples of this can be seen from Diageo’s Guinness Open Gate Brewery in London stating plans to give away 100 free beers at its Old Brewer's Yard site in Covent Garden today (7 August) as well as AB InBev launching a global ‘Cheers to Beer’ campaign timed to coincide with IBD to celebrate the “role beer plays in culture and communities around the world.” On the other side of the world, Korea-based Oriental Brewery held a staff brewing event this week at its Icheon brewery in Gyeonggi as a way to boost celebrations of IBD. Closer to home, airport hospitality business Plaza Premium Group (PPG) has celebrated the date by partnering with Asahi to bring Asahi Super Dry and Meantime Dial Lager to its airport lounges in the UK.

Celebrating and connecting

Speaking about IBD and the way people connect over a beer, AB InBev CEO Michel Doukeris said: “Beer is universal and woven into cultures and communities around the world. No matter who you are, what you do for a living, or where you live, when someone says, ‘Let’s grab a beer,’ you know it means something more. It’s an invitation to celebrate or to simply connect.” In London’s Islington, Godet, the Essex Road listening bar, will mark IBD with a tap takeover from Bristol's Lost and Grounded brewers, while in India Medusa Beverages has rolled out a new digital campaign celebrating beer, friendship and memorable stories. Describing the celebratory day’s global importance, Brewers Association of New Zealand executive director Dylan Firth explained: “Beer has always been about bringing people together, whether it’s catching up with friends at the local, enjoying a barbecue, watching your favourite team, or discovering a new brewery” and added that “International Beer Day is a great opportunity to celebrate” brewing culture. To celebrate IBD all over the world, beer experts are also partaking in a range of brews. For instance, beer sommelier, international beer judge, and certified cicerone Paul Davies told db he will be in one of the oldest bars in the world in Belgium "tasting all six editions of the Cafe Vlissinghe house beer". Ukrainian beer educator Lana Svitankova revealed to db that she will be in Lewes in East Sussex for this year's IBD and so is going to indulge in "something from Harveys or Beak for sure" and added: "Maybe both, why choose?"

title: Pub group dives into Notting Hill Carnival history
summary:
The Metropolitan Pub Company, which owns 60 venues across London, Manchester, Bath and Glasgow, will stage a series of events this month celebrating the 60th anniversary of Notting Hill Carnival.

The post Pub group dives into Notting Hill Carnival history appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
The Metropolitan Pub Company, which owns 60 venues across London, Manchester, Bath and Glasgow, will stage a series of events this month celebrating the 60th anniversary of Notting Hill Carnival. Taking place across London pubs The Ladbroke Arms, The Mitre and The Prince Bonaparte during August, the events programme forms part of Carnival 60, a six-month heritage initiative raising awareness of the origins, history and lasting cultural impact of Notting Hill Carnival. Live poetry readings, calypso music, guided rum tastings and walking tours exploring local Caribbean history are all part of the initiative. “Carnival 60 is an opportunity to celebrate the people, places and stories that have shaped Notting Hill Carnival over six decades,” said Yvette Reinfor, founder and director of London-based community interest company More Curricular CIC. “By partnering with Metropolitan Pub Company, we’re able to bring those stories to wider audiences in our community, where people can learn more about the heritage and cultural significance of Carnival.”

Rooted in communities

Vincent Madden, director of Metropolitan Pub Company, added: “We believe that great pubs are rooted in the communities they serve. These events are an opportunity to celebrate the history and cultural richness of West London while supporting an important community organisation.” Notting Hill Carnival first began as a response to racial tension and violence in London, including the 1958 Notting Hill race riots and the racist murder of Antiguan man Kelso Cochrane. Trinidadian activist and newspaper editor Claudia Jones, now known as the 'Mother of Notting Hill Carnival', organised an indoor Caribbean Carnival at St Pancras Town Hall in Camden in January 1959 to help improve relations in the area. The televised indoor event featured steel bands, calypso music, and dancing to boost morale and showcase West Indian culture. By 1966 the event had moved outdoors as the brainchild of social worker Rhaune Laslett, who persuaded a local steel band to travel through the streets playing steel pan music. As the troupe progressed along Portobello Road, local residents gathered to dance, transforming the occasion into a celebration, and marking the start of what we today know as Carnival. Notting Hill Carnival takes place this year from Saturday 29 August to Monday 31 August 31, and the Metropolitan Pub Company events line-up includes: The Prince Bonaparte, Westbourne Park – 4 August Carnival is 60. What Next? will bring together Ansel Wong CBE and guest speakers for a panel discussion exploring the future of Carnival over the next 60 years and will also feature live poetry readings and calypso music. The Mitre, Holland Park – 11 August Guests will take part in a guided tasting of Bumbu, the Barbadian rum brand, discovering its history and Caribbean roots through a curated tasting experience. The Ladbroke Arms, Notting Hill – 25 August A 90-minute guided walking tour led by Yvette Reinfor will explore hidden local histories and celebrate the Caribbean community that played a key role in shaping Notting Hill Carnival. The walk ends at The Ladbroke Arms with a fish and chip taster and a half pint of the pub's House Ale.

Big boost

As the drinks business reported, Carnival can offer a big boost for drinks brands with research group Williams determining that domestic visitors spend an estimated £58.5 million on food and drinks alone during Notting Hill Carnival, while international visitors add £20.3m to this. Rum brand Duppy Share told db that it sold more than 2,000 bottles of rum and 4,000 canned cocktails over four days at the 2024 Notting Hill Carnival. Not only can the event increase the visibility of brands, it also offers the chance to offer collectible versions of favourite drinks linked to Carnival. Last year, Hennessy debuted its own float at Notting Hill Carnival alongside a limited-edition bottle of Hennessy V.S, swapping the label’s traditional gold scrollwork for a bold feather motif inspired by Carnival colours and energy.

title: Exploring eight EU wine regions set to win over drinkers
summary:
The EU is at the heart of the international wine trade, with its position built on quality assurance and regulation. A recent masterclass explored how that is driving innovation in its emerging regions.

The post Exploring eight EU wine regions set to win over drinkers appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
The EU is at the heart of the international wine trade, with its position built on quality assurance and regulation. A recent masterclass explored how that is driving innovation in its emerging regions. Those working in the UK wine trade will be used to tastings highlighting a single winery’s portfolio. They may have attended masterclasses surveying a producers association, a popular grape variety or, perhaps, a wider region. A recent masterclass in Cardiff, however, took a grander view. Although it surveyed a number of wines through the lenses of variety and region, its theme was significantly larger: the strength of the entire EU as a wine-producing bloc. In that endeavour, Neil McAndrew served as guide. During 35 years in the wine trade, he has worked across retail, distribution and fine wine, in addition to a current role advising the EU’s ‘More Than Only Food & Drink’ campaign. Over that time he has – quite literally – seen the EU grow, with new nations joining, bringing indigenous varieties and traditional winemaking. He believes the EU’s wine scene is stronger than ever. “There’s no doubt that the EU is in a fantastic position in terms of the breadth of producers, styles of wine and grape varieties,” he commented. “It is absolutely the epicentre of wine production in the world.” That is more than just a statement of Europe’s size. Although geographical spread is important, just as vital is the structure under which EU wine is produced. According to the European Parliament’s 2023 briefing on the EU wine sector, 65% of wine in the EU is made under a Protected Designation of Origin (PDO). This means that production, processing and preparation must take place within a specific geographical area, and under stipulated guidelines to match the regional style. A further 17% falls under a Protected Geographical Indication (PGI), meaning that at least one of those processes must take place in the geographical area. The EU also has its own certification for organic production. These programmes matter because they underpin the EU’s unique offering. Across its wines – indeed, across its other food and drink products – they contribute three pillars that offer the consumer confidence: authenticity, sustainability and quality.

What marks out EU wine?

The PDO and PGI schemes mean that consumers can trust what is in the bottle. On a very basic level, that means assurances of product safety and traceable origin. Yet more and more, consumers are recognising the schemes as custodians of heritage, and promoters of forward-thinking winemaking When it comes to authenticity, the EU has a significant advantage over other wine-producing regions. With the PDO and PGI systems to promote regional specialities, its producers have ample opportunities to lean into their local identity. As Europe is the home of Vitis vinifera, the bloc has a huge wealth of native grapes to showcase. By prioritising those varieties, as well as distinctive terroirs and Europe’s remarkable stock of old vines, the EU has a strong trajectory that does not rely on replicating the same styles in every region. PDOs and PGIs protect local traditions and mean that consumers come to recognise their distinctiveness and seek out such wines. In fact, McAndrew identified a number of emerging consumer trends that will benefit EU producers in coming years: island wines with unique terroirs, Central European nations with indigenous grapes, and expertise with hybrid grapes to protect against climate change. As more UK businesses get wise to the diversity of EU production, especially in the on-trade and in the speciality off-trade, these trends represent a key commercial opportunity. Sustainability has proved a further advantage for EU producers. Through its schemes – notably the EU’s organic certification, but also through some PDOs and PGIs mandating sustainable production – the EU is making sure that consumers have highly sustainable options when buying wine. The organic certification, for instance, limits the use of pesticides and promotes animal welfare in production. Organic wines now make commercial sense, as well as ethical sense, McAndrew explained. “The category is expected to grow 10% every year to 2030, and that’s quite significant, given where we’re coming from,” he said. “A lot of organic wine comes from France, Spain and Italy, but Greece, Bulgaria and Romania are all in the top 20 organic wine regions in the world.” (Citing data sourced from FiBL and IFOAM’s The World of Organic Agriculture 2026.) As for quality, that was on show in the second part of McAndrew’s masterclass. Taking eight wines from across the EU as his starting point, he demonstrated how those principles translate from an EU-wide structure to great wines from exciting origins.

Landwein der Saar PGI, Germany

McAndrew began with this PGI, which presented one of Europe’s most recognisable grape varieties in an unexpected context. The example he chose was a Sekt made with Riesling grown in the Saar’s steep slate vineyards, demonstrating this grape variety’s potential in traditional method sparkling winemaking. Sourced from vines that are more than 100 years old, the wine showed the concentration possible from long-lived vineyards, while 12 months of lees ageing contributed a creamy mousse. Elegant, mineral and bone-dry, it lived up to the region’s characteristic intensity without being too heavy.

Κρασοχωρια Λεμεσου PDO, Cyprus

This Cypriot PDO (also known as the Wine Villages of Limassol), which spans high-altitude sites, allows a number of grape varieties, but the local Xynisteri is a standout. The white grape now accounts for 23% of the country’s vineyards (according to ampelographic tome Wine Grapes). Although historically associated with Commandaria dessert wine, elegant dry white examples are increasingly gaining ground. McAndrew presented one such wine, which showed off its citrus and spice notes, as well as a broad texture from maturation on the lees. The wine was also certified organic, a further tick for customers looking to drink authentic wines that protect their historic landscapes.

Tokaj PDO, Hungary

The PDO wines of Tokaj (or Tokaji, depending on your preference) need little introduction among wine lovers; decadently sweet botrytised examples have firmly placed them in the fine wine pantheon. Yet the area’s dry wines, particularly those based on Furmint (as was shown in the masterclass) prove the value of indigenous grape varieties. With characteristic acidity and vineyards on volcanic soils, the wines typically have freshness and energy. This allows for versatility: the acidity can be embraced with a zesty fruit profile, or played against waxiness and a touch of residual sugar for added weight.

Πλαγιεσ Αιγιαλειασ PGI, Greece

In the northern Peloponnese, you can find a fantastic combination of high-altitude sites (sometimes more than 1,000 metres above sea level) and coastal breezes. This PGI, also known as Slopes of Aigialeia, makes full use of those freshening influences. The PGI regulations allow producers some choice in grape varieties, but in Cardiff an unusual local speciality was given the spotlight. McAndrew presented a wine made with Lagorthi, a weighty, lightly aromatic variety, that had been vinified with fermentation on the skins and some clay amphorae ageing for added texture.

Murfatlar PDO, Romania

“Wines like this are the future,” McAndrew enthused, as he introduced a Fetească Neagră from the Romanian PDO. The region certainly has much to commend it: in sunny vineyards near the Black Sea, it creates intense, concentrated wines. Fetească Neagră, meanwhile, is drought- and cold-resistant, providing growers with reassurance in changing climatic conditions. The example shown was treated as many international fine red wines are, with careful oak ageing to integrate flavours and foster velvety tannins. The estate is the first to gain biodynamic certification in Romania, a further selling point.

Stredoslovenská PDO, Slovakia

Also known as Stredoslovenský or Stredoslovenské, this Slovakian region was the northernmost on display at the masterclass. The grape variety Frankovka is a true Central European speciality, and may be known to consumers as Austria’s Blaufränkisch. Although consumers may consider it an emerging region for wine, the volcanic hills have a viticultural heritage dating back to Roman times. McAndrew selected a bottle that fully embraced the bright cherry fruit, peppery spice and crunchy quality of the grape variety. With eight months spent in oak, it can offer an alternative to Chianti for the interested consumer.

Мелник PDO, Bulgaria

Situated in the valley of the Struma River in Bulgaria’s southwest, Мелник PDO (also known as Melnik PDO), enjoys a Mediterranean climate and vineyards combining sand and limestone. It is named after its grapes: there are, in fact, two Melnik varieties, one of which ripens early and the other late. The local varieties, which have long histories in the region, lend themselves to serious winemaking, as McAndrew’s audience discovered in a low-intervention, biodynamic example based on the early-ripening variety. He compared it to Syrah and Nebbiolo, particularly with 15 months in new French and Bulgarian barriques lending polish to the wine.

Utiel-Requena PDO, Spain

Just as the session began with an unexpected wine from a well-known wine-producing nation, so did it close. Utiel-Requena PDO proves that Spain has more to offer than Tempranillo; the Valencian region has made local variety Bobal its calling card. Among its chief assets is a wealth of old vines, lending concentration and tannic richness. Its bold, flavourful reds further benefit from a high-altitude plateau, contributing generous, ripe flavours, while the dry climate reduces disease pressure and means organic viticulture is common, as in the wine that McAndrew presented.

title: Lewis bets on Guinness and RTDs in Diageo recovery strategy
summary:
Sir Dave Lewis is going deep with cost cutting at Diageo, but he is also intent on restructuring the business to unlock greater value from its portfolio, writes Ron Emler.

The post Lewis bets on Guinness and RTDs in Diageo recovery strategy appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Sir Dave Lewis is going deep with cost cutting at Diageo, but he is also intent on restructuring the business to unlock greater value from its portfolio, writes Ron Emler.

Lewis said the company would continue to focus on premiumisation. “It's done very well for us,” he says, but his recovery plan also envisages some price adjustments. That, however, is only part of what he sees as being “competitive and returning to a norm”. “I'm talking about brand strength, quality of brand mixers, innovation.  Some of the pricing through Covid has got a little bit out of whack, and and we've adjusted some of those things."

'Drastic' Dave?

Lewis hates the nickname “Drastic” (earned from his days at Unilever and Tesco) and despite overseeing a swathe of job losses as duplicated roles are eliminated across the business, he is intent on developing the entire portfolio. “We are not hawking any of our brands”, he says, but vows to make them all work for shareholders. “We intend to activate a portfolio, so that we can serve more customers on more occasions.” Far from selling off Guinness, as some have speculated, a US$1 billion investment to double Guinness production capacity over the next five years is central to his plans, as he takes it deeper into global markets. The future for Guinness [which now makes up about 12% of group sales] is “very bright”.

Betting on RTDs

He wants to make up lost ground in the RTD market. Having once held almost a quarter of that sector Diageo now has about 10%. “We’re just going to roll up our sleeves and get on with our own business,” he says. He is especially critical of Diageo’s whiskey offerings in the RTD market. “We have not put our best foot forward in whiskey RTDs; I’m disappointed with the flavours”, he says, referring largely to Crown Royal. Change has already started with a US$20 million investment in a plant in the US, much of which will be devoted to expanding Crown Royal's presence in the fast-growing market for smaller pack formats while broadening its flavour range.

Premium pre-mixed

Lewis also argued that if around half of Scotch and other whiskies are consumed in mixed drinks, there is a significant opportunity to offer more premium ready-to-drink whisky serves. The US market is critical to Diageo, accounting for more than 35% of its global sales. Turning it around is the responsibility of new head John O’Keefe, who acknowledges that the group has seen “share declines across around 65% of our business” in America. He identifies Crown Royal, Smirnoff, Captain Morgan and Don Julio as the brands requiring the greatest attention, with poor packaging, weak marketing execution and non-availability of the right smaller pack sizes as key to their woes.

Restructuring for US growth

Lewis is backing him to put that right but knows that it will take at least two years to bring Diageo’s US market back to growth, even though O’Keefe is restructuring the business model. "We are moving from separate Spirits and Beer divisions to a single commercial organisation, with one commercial leader, one set of support functions and one set of key accounts. That is going to improve our agility immensely,” O’Keefe says. And notably Lewis points out that not one of O’Keefe’s plans for the US market involves crude price cuts. “There have been some weaknesses in our core brands for a number of years that have been covered up [by the growth of tequila]. That’s why we have lost share in North America. “These are very big, important brands which frankly we have not done a great job with. We need to go back and do that and also to recover the momentum with tequila. “We are confident we know how to do that, but it won’t be overnight”, says Lewis.

title: Wildfires scorch wine tourism in Bordeaux
summary:
Although the Gironde's catastrophic wildfires spared most vineyards from damage, they drove away visitors, impacted revenues and exposed the vulnerability of Bordeaux's hospitality sector at the height of the tourist season. db reports.

The post Wildfires scorch wine tourism in Bordeaux appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Although the Gironde's catastrophic wildfires spared most vineyards from damage, they drove away visitors, impacted revenues and exposed the vulnerability of Bordeaux's hospitality sector at the height of the tourist season. db reports. Last week, thousands of French firefighters battled blazes that burned an area four times the size of Paris in the Gironde region. It’s the largest wildfire the region has seen since 1949, and the worst crisis the country has tackled, according to President Emmanuel Macron, since World War II. Winemakers even joined the fire-fighting efforts, mobilising equipment and manpower to help snuff the flames that not only scorched 42,000 hectares of land, but also stung the economy, and put pressure on a wine sector already squeezed by soaring costs and a drop in global demand.  In one sense, the region’s world-renowned wineries have dodged the worst of it: vineyards were far away enough to see any real damage, and the quality of the 2026 vintage is unlikely to be impacted by smoke taint, winemakers tell the drinks business. However, the wine tourism sector has not escaped unscathed, with some 224,000 people evacuating the region, including a spate of tourists. 

Wine tourism suffers

Oliver Cazevanne saw many cancellations across his two bed-and-breakfast sites at his winery, Château de Bel, situated in Arveyres on the banks of the Dordogne river, despite the fact that smoke only covered the area for just one day.  “Since the fires we have suffered a huge loss of income from tourism,” adds Château La Rame’s Augustin Allo – Armand. “As holidaymakers have deserted the region out of fear, we are seeing a massive drop in visitor numbers, and the restaurants in the Arcachon Basin with whom we work are reporting a more than significant decline in trade. This will undoubtedly have an impact on the sale of our wines in these establishments.” Peggy Plouhinec, managing director at Château Picque Caillou, also saw a drop in visitor numbers. However, she adds:  “Luckily, the smoke didn't stick around long enough to have an impact on us, especially since we had over 15mm of rain right after. Also, harvest is still quite a way off, so we aren't worried about smoke taint for the grapes.” Much attention has been credited to the risk of smoke taint in Bordeaux, which occurs when compounds released by wildfire smoke are absorbed into grape skins. During red wine fermentation, these compounds can be extracted from the skins, potentially giving wines undesirable smoky, ashy or medicinal flavours. 

Smoke taint 'not necessarily a cause for concern'

But smoke taint proves a sticky debate in the wine world. “There’s very little established scientific evidence to date of smoke taint being passed to vines that are not in close proximity to the fire itself — and at present the nearest vineyards are at around 15km from the source of the smoke to which they are exposed,” the drinks business’ Bordeaux correspondent previously told db. “Some vineyards are geographically closer, but the smoke they have experienced has come from further away due to the prevailing wind direction.”  Marine Martin, international PR for the Conseil Interprofessionnel du Vin Bordeaux (CIVB), assures that across the region’s wine growing regions, no impact on grape quality has been observed.  “Unfortunately, wildfires are no longer unfamiliar events in our region, which means that we now have some experience in assessing their potential effects with a reasonable degree of confidence,” she told db. “Based on the information currently available, we do not have any particular concerns regarding the quality of the forthcoming vintage.” She cited scientific research to support her claims: “Smoke itself is not necessarily a cause for concern. Research has shown that smoke taint results from the uptake of specific volatile phenolic compounds, and the risk depends on a combination of factors including proximity, duration of exposure and stage of ripening.  “At this point in the season, harvest remains several weeks away and the grapes are only at the beginning to mid-veraison stage. During this period, the berry skin acts as a natural protective barrier, significantly limiting the absorption of smoke-derived compounds.”

Cité du Vin: 'the economic effects were immediate'

And chateaux were not the only businesses impacted in the wine sector. In the city of Bordeaux, the celebrated interactive wine museum, Cité du Vin, which teeters over the city like a swirling wine glass, was also hit hard in terms of trade. While the cultural centre, which toasts its 10th anniversary this year, only had to close one hour early on one day due to the smell of smoke, visitor numbers sharply dropped. “Some roads were closed, trains were cancelled, and the Government advised against travelling to the region,” said Solène Jaboulet, marketing and communications director at the museum which toasts its 10th anniversary this year. Until 25 July, visitor numbers were the same as last year’s, but they suddenly dropped by 60% through the end of July. “The economic effects were immediate as well,” Jaboulet added. “80% of our revenue comes from visitor spending (70% from the ticket sales and 10% from the gift shop). So you can easily imagine the economic impact.” But now, she’s relieved to see tourism rebounding. “We welcome more visitors every day, all of whom are delighted with their visit. The region is safe and beautiful and we encourage all lovers of France and wine to come along.”

title: Fero and Bevica link-up ‘significant step’ to boost customers’ operational efficiency
summary:
Fintech platform Fero has partnered with drinks software management system Bevica to give both companies customers a more joined-up way to manage the operational and financial sides of their businesses.

The post Fero and Bevica link-up ‘significant step’ to boost customers’ operational efficiency appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content: Fintech platform Fero has partnered with drinks software management system Bevica to give both companies customers a more joined-up way to manage the operational and financial sides of their businesses. Bevica The connection of the two systems means stock data can pass between the two automatically, with Bevica customers gaining easier access to Fero’s funding and supply chain support wherever they need it. This results in “a more complete platform for drinks business at every stage of growth,” Fero said. Meanwhile, Fero customers can use the Bevica software to keep their operational data up to date without manual syncing or re-entering it, removing “an operational friction point”, it said. According to Fero, the partnership marks a significant step forward for both companies, as it removes duplication from the system that has arisen from the “fragmented technology” that exists across the broader drinks industry without requiring a high level of customisation or cost to integrate. The link-up aims to reduce admin work for clients who use both platforms, with orders created in Bevica syncing automatically - and in real time - with Fero. Bevica explained that any orders are entered into its platform will be shared automatically with Fero, giving businesses a "clear, consistent view of their stock, sales and financial position at all times", as well as faster access to funding decisions when needed. Paul Wellingham, CEO of Bevica said the company had always been about helping drinks businesses run their day-to-day operations properly. “This integration with the Fero platform builds on that by removing manual steps and joining things up behind the scenes,” he said. “This will give our customers access to funding and supply chain support without changing how they already work. It’s a practical step that will make a real difference.” Mitchel Fowler, CEO of Fero said he was excited to make the Fero platform available to Bevica’s clients in the UK drinks trade, noting that it would add “working capital management and supply chain efficiency seamlessly [to] augment their existing systems and processes."

title: This historic Polish distillery could be yours
summary:
In the heart of Hanseatic Szczecin, Starka SFW – a brand and distillery site going to auction this year – offers a unique opportunity to revive a heritage spirit and redevelop a site dating to the 19th century.

The post This historic Polish distillery could be yours appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
In the heart of Hanseatic Szczecin, Starka SFW – a brand and distillery site going to auction this year – offers a unique opportunity to revive a heritage spirit and redevelop a site dating to the 19th century. A distillery is never truly down and out. While the alcohol industry can be volatile and sites temporarily shuttered, careful management will often see a revival of once-closed sites. Indeed, a period of inactivity can often remind consumers of the quality they have missed. Examples abound. Take Brora, Port Ellen and Rosebank distilleries in Scotland: having been mothballed for decades, they are now making whisky again. In other segments, you find heritage brands given a new lease of life, such as Langs Rum, Chicken Cock Whiskey and Sazerac de Forge & Fils Cognac. Rarely, however, does an opportunity appear with as much heritage as Starka. That is the emblematic product of Polish distillery SFW Starka, founded in the historic port city of Szczecin in 1863. The product is distinctive, sitting between categories. It is an aged rye spirit flavoured with small quantities of select botanicals, giving it characteristics of vodka, whisky and traditional European flavoured spirits. Due to a period of mismanagement and litigation, Starka has not been bottling in the last few years. Yet the distillery is being carefully maintained, and therefore is ready for a new owner to realise its substantial potential. The sale package represents a significant bundle: it comes with associated intellectual property, operational production facilities, cellars full of ageing spirits, and development rights across portions of the site. Rather than think of it as a simple distillery asset, its spokesperson David Lesperance believes that the brand is a rich story in its own right: “Starka is more like a cat with nine lives.”

Centuries of history

As a business, Starka has already proved its resilience. Lesperance divides its story into distinct phases. “Its first life was very fulfilling and lasted a few centuries,” he explains. That is a succinct summary of a remarkable story. The spirit dates to at least the 15th century and comes with its share of traditions – for instance, a barrel would often be filled to mark a birth and only opened on that child’s eventual wedding day. The Starka distillery was constructed in 1863, an impressive monument to the local spirit. Its good fortune carried into the 20th Century. “Its second life was during the Communist period where it continued to thrive due to its extraordinary product – aged amber vodka – that was famous throughout the region,” Lesperance says. However, more recent history provided a turn in fortunes. It did, however, fare better than competitors: Starka is now the only producer of the eponymous spirit. “Its third life was in the post-Communist period when it struggled to survive due to lack of qualified management,” says Lesperance. Then, its fourth life arrived when Lesperance and his group invested and refocused the core business on aged vodka, though its fifth life followed under a local owner who “saw Starka as a golden goose and tried to extract too many eggs”. Starka’s next life beckons as Lesperance works to find a buyer that fits perfectly with the brand. “We are looking to attract a buyer who will recognise and appreciate the remarkable product, history and opportunities represented by Starka,” he comments.

A wealth of opportunities

Starka does not offer a commonplace investment, the kind of brand that seems identical to many others. Instead, it is a unique proposition with a wealth of development opportunities. Vodka is a category that is on the up. In the US, the Wine & Spirits Wholesalers of America’s SipSource tool estimates the vodka category will outperform the core spirits market over the next 12 months. Aside from the opportunity to keep making the emblematic product, Starka’s immense reserves provide a historical bounty is ready to drink. The cellars are full of ageing barrels of Starka to be bottled as premium products. That includes more than 50,000 litres aged for at least 33 years. There are also exceptionally rare heritage barrels, dating back as far as 1947. One of them, barrel 45, is believed to be filled with distillate from 1947-1956, professionally valued at Polish złoty 123,841,433 (approximately £24 million/US$23.2m). Thinking more broadly, investors can expand revenue streams thanks to the remarkable building and its position. The distillery is in the heart of the historic Hanseatic city, and previously attracted 10,000 visitors each year with minimal promotional activity. Spirits tourism is an area that could see substantial growth, particularly as there are direct rail links to Warsaw and Berlin, the latter of which is receiving a major upgrade. In addition to the heritage production facilities, the complex has broader development opportunities. A prior-approved redevelopment project for the site included five multi-family residential buildings (containing 316 apartments), 584 square metres of commercial space, and 322 parking spaces. To fully explain the opportunities on offer, Starka is hosting a webinar next week for potential buyers and real estate developers. The session, at 3pm BST on Tuesday 11 August, will run through the history and potential of the site. To sign up for this webinar, click here. For a behind-the-scenes look at the distillery and its opportunities, check out the video below.  https://vimeo.com/1215433142?fl=pl&fe=sh

title: 67 Pall Mall Shanghai wants to boost the profile of Chinese wine
summary:
As the countdown begins to the December opening of London wine club 67 Pall Mall's Shanghai location, founder and CEO Grant Ashton tells Joyce Yip why he believes Shanghai, "the world's most important wine market", has the potential to elevate the global profile of Chinese wine.

The post 67 Pall Mall Shanghai wants to boost the profile of Chinese wine appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
As the countdown begins to the December opening of London wine club 67 Pall Mall's Shanghai location, founder and CEO Grant Ashton tells Joyce Yip why he believes Shanghai, "the world's most important wine market", has the potential to elevate the global profile of Chinese wine. Just three years after it cut the ribbon to a bar residency in Hong Kong, 67 Pall Mall will open this December a wine club in Shanghai – a city CEO and founder Grant Ashton deems the “most important wine market in the world”.  The Shanghai club will also be among the group’s most expensive to join. Until December, annual membership is priced at RMB38,000 (£4,184) sans joining fee, which will increase to RMB50,000 (£5,500) with a joining fee, though Ashton didn’t specify how much. For comparison, 67 Pall Mall’s London, Singapore and Verbier locations charge a yearly £2,750 (with a £2,000 joining fee); S$4,800 (£2,772, with a £1,150 joining fee) and CHF 2,500 (£2,307 with a £1,846 joining fee), respectively.  The new club opens as rival Hong Kong-based wine club Club Bâtard prepares to launch its own Shanghai outpost a month earlier. Memberships are now opened at a one-time joining fee of RMB100,000 (£11,000) with a monthly subscription of RMB1,250 (£137).  Ashton said 67 Pall Mall’s appeal lies in its “combination of expertise, scale, provenance and community”, adding that the Shanghai club’s capped membership of 1,500 should drive demand. The club will also offer what Ashton describes as its “most extensive wine selection in China”, featuring 5000-plus wines from more than 40 countries, with around 1000 available by the glass. 

What to expect

Nestled in a century-old French Renaissance Maison, the multi-floor 67 Pall Mall Shanghai will include a baijiu bar alongside the whisky and spirits offerings, plus “more private rooms than any other 67 Pall Mall Club, because private dining is central to how people entertain,” says Ashton.  A dedicated cellar will hold more than 1,000 labels of fine Chinese wine, including rare, aged and collectible bottles from producers in Ningxia, Xinjiang, Yunnan and beyond. Ashton said the club aims to present Chinese wine with the same seriousness and respect afforded to Bordeaux and Burgundy, rather than as a niche category. “Chinese winemaking is producing bottles of genuine world-class quality now, and most of the world hasn’t caught up to that yet. We want Shanghai to be part of changing that,” he says.  When 67 Pall Mall opened in Hong Kong in January 2024, its Hollywood Road address was only meant to be temporary as the team searched for a permanent home in the city. With the latest spotlight on Shanghai, Ashton didn’t indicate what lies ahead for its Hong Kong location, only that it “plays a very specific role” as “one of the great wine hubs of Asia” and “the gateway into China for the wine trade”.

title: Wine writer Matthew Jukes dies aged 58
summary:
Matthew Jukes, one of Britain's best-known wine writers, critics and drinks entrepreneurs, has died suddenly while on holiday with his family in Portugal.

The post Wine writer Matthew Jukes dies aged 58 appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Matthew Jukes, one of Britain's best-known wine writers, critics and drinks entrepreneurs, has died suddenly while on holiday with his family in Portugal. He was 58.

Jukes died on 6 August. He is survived by his wife, Amelia, their sons, Rollo and Victor, and his daughters, Isadora and Elspeth. Few figures have enjoyed such a varied and influential career in wine. A gifted communicator with an infectious enthusiasm for the subject, Jukes spent almost four decades introducing consumers and professionals alike to the pleasures of wine through restaurants, newspapers, books, and broadcasting. His career began in 1987, aged just 19, when he joined Barnes Wine Shop in London, working alongside wine consultant James Rogers. Three years later he became wine buyer at the renowned London restaurant Bibendum, a role he held for 26 years, earning widespread recognition for one of Britain's most celebrated restaurant wine lists.

Wit and warmth

Alongside his work in hospitality, Jukes established himself as one of the UK's most recognisable wine broadcasters and journalists. He presented BBC radio programmes, hosted Channel 4's Wine Hunt, and became a familiar voice explaining wine with warmth, wit and remarkable accessibility. He was also a prolific author, writing 14 books, including The Wine Book, which was later serialised by the Daily Mail. He subsequently wrote the newspaper's weekly wine column in the Weekend magazine for 22 years, while also contributing a long-running column to MoneyWeek for more than two decades. Although his expertise extended across the wine world, Jukes became particularly associated with Australian wine. In recognition of his contribution to promoting Australian producers internationally, he received the Honorary Australian of the Year Award in 2012.

Drinks entrepreneur

His entrepreneurial ambitions extended beyond journalism. During the mid-1990s he co-owned the acclaimed Fulham Road wine bar The Crescent with the late wine merchant Hilary Gibbs. More recently he founded JUKES Cordialities, a range of premium non-alcoholic botanical drinks designed to accompany food, a business that had just secured investment from Whispering Angel creator Sacha Lichine. What distinguished Jukes throughout his career was his ability to communicate with every type of wine drinker. His tasting notes managed to satisfy experienced collectors while remaining approachable and entertaining for newcomers. He combined deep technical knowledge with an infectious sense of curiosity and genuine excitement about discovering great bottles, whether inexpensive everyday wines or the world's finest labels.

Devoted family man

Away from wine, he was equally passionate about food, hospitality and sport, particularly rugby, a game in which he excelled during his school years. Friends and colleagues also knew him as an energetic host, a tireless traveller and someone whose enthusiasm for sharing food and wine was matched only by his devotion to his family. Matthew Jukes leaves behind an extraordinary legacy. As a writer, broadcaster, buyer and entrepreneur, he helped influence how a generation of consumers thought about wine while maintaining a deep understanding of every part of the trade, from restaurant lists and retail shelves to brand building and production. Tributes from across the wine world are certain to reflect the respect and affection in which he was held. For now, however, the drinks industry is left mourning the loss of one of its brightest and most distinctive voices.

title: E&A Scheer names Mitch Wilson as head of global rum development
summary:
Global rum specialist and supplier E&A Scheer has appointed Mitch Wilson to the newly created role of head of global rum development.

The post E&A Scheer names Mitch Wilson as head of global rum development appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Global rum specialist and supplier E&A Scheer has appointed Mitch Wilson to the newly created role of head of global rum development. Wilson joins E&A Scheer with nearly 15 years of experience in the rum category, including international ambassador roles with Maison Ferrand and Black Tot Rum. Based in Amsterdam, Wilson is set to lead the commercial growth of the group’s single cask programme, support bespoke rum projects and help expand category education as part of E&A Scheer’s commercial team.

Investment

Speaking about the hire, E&A Scheer CEO and chief rum officer Carsten Vlierboom said: “The future of rum lies in quality, authenticity and long-term partnerships. We’re continuing to invest in the premium end of the category and in the expertise that helps our customers succeed. Mitch’s experience complements our technical knowledge and strengthens our ability to help customers create extraordinary products and brands.” Wilson explained: “I’ve spent nearly 15 years exploring every stage of the rum journey, from distilleries and production to hospitality, retail, education and global brand building. Joining E&A Scheer is an opportunity to apply that experience at the source, helping customers make smarter decisions from cask selection and blend development through to the finished product. Together, we can combine unrivalled access to outstanding Rum with commercial insight to help build stronger brands and continue elevating the category.”

Integration

As part of its continued investment in high-end rum, E&A Scheer has revealed that it is also further integrating its internationally recognised single cask rum specialist, The Main Rum Company, into its Amsterdam operations, bringing its expertise and  inventory under one roof. While The Main Rum Company label will continue to serve those sourcing single cask rums, the company has highlighted that the integration creates "a more streamlined destination for high-quality aged stocks and rare single casks".

title: Reasons to celebrate International Beer Day
summary:
The global celebration International Beer Day is held annually on the first Friday of August. db raises a glass to the initiative.

The post Reasons to celebrate International Beer Day appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
The global celebration International Beer Day is held annually on the first Friday of August. db raises a glass to the initiative. International Beer Day (IBD) was founded back in 2007 in Santa Cruz, California and began as a way of bringing people together to enjoy great drinks, thank local staff, and celebrate global brewing traditions. August was chosen for its summer weather and distance from other beer celebrations, and the event spans more than 200 cities globally. Now, brewers and beer venues are using the date to springboard their own campaigns and marketing activities. Examples of this can be seen from Diageo’s Guinness Open Gate Brewery in London stating plans to give away 100 free beers at its Old Brewer's Yard site in Covent Garden today (7 August) as well as AB InBev launching a global ‘Cheers to Beer’ campaign timed to coincide with IBD to celebrate the “role beer plays in culture and communities around the world.” On the other side of the world, Korea-based Oriental Brewery held a staff brewing event this week at its Icheon brewery in Gyeonggi as a way to boost celebrations of IBD. Closer to home, airport hospitality business Plaza Premium Group (PPG) has celebrated the date by partnering with Asahi to bring Asahi Super Dry and Meantime Dial Lager to its airport lounges in the UK.

Celebrating and connecting

Speaking about IBD and the way people connect over a beer, AB InBev CEO Michel Doukeris said: “Beer is universal and woven into cultures and communities around the world. No matter who you are, what you do for a living, or where you live, when someone says, ‘Let’s grab a beer,’ you know it means something more. It’s an invitation to celebrate or to simply connect.” In London’s Islington, Godet, the Essex Road listening bar, will mark IBD with a tap takeover from Bristol's Lost and Grounded brewers, while in India Medusa Beverages has rolled out a new digital campaign celebrating beer, friendship and memorable stories. Describing the celebratory day’s global importance, Brewers Association of New Zealand executive director Dylan Firth explained: “Beer has always been about bringing people together, whether it’s catching up with friends at the local, enjoying a barbecue, watching your favourite team, or discovering a new brewery” and added that “International Beer Day is a great opportunity to celebrate” brewing culture. To celebrate IBD all over the world, beer experts are also partaking in a range of brews. For instance, beer sommelier, international beer judge, and certified cicerone Paul Davies told db he will be in one of the oldest bars in the world in Belgium "tasting all six editions of the Cafe Vlissinghe house beer". Ukrainian beer educator Lana Svitankova revealed to db that she will be in Lewes in East Sussex for this year's IBD and so is going to indulge in "something from Harveys or Beak for sure" and added: "Maybe both, why choose?"

title: Pub group dives into Notting Hill Carnival history
summary:
The Metropolitan Pub Company, which owns 60 venues across London, Manchester, Bath and Glasgow, will stage a series of events this month celebrating the 60th anniversary of Notting Hill Carnival.

The post Pub group dives into Notting Hill Carnival history appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
The Metropolitan Pub Company, which owns 60 venues across London, Manchester, Bath and Glasgow, will stage a series of events this month celebrating the 60th anniversary of Notting Hill Carnival. Taking place across London pubs The Ladbroke Arms, The Mitre and The Prince Bonaparte during August, the events programme forms part of Carnival 60, a six-month heritage initiative raising awareness of the origins, history and lasting cultural impact of Notting Hill Carnival. Live poetry readings, calypso music, guided rum tastings and walking tours exploring local Caribbean history are all part of the initiative. “Carnival 60 is an opportunity to celebrate the people, places and stories that have shaped Notting Hill Carnival over six decades,” said Yvette Reinfor, founder and director of London-based community interest company More Curricular CIC. “By partnering with Metropolitan Pub Company, we’re able to bring those stories to wider audiences in our community, where people can learn more about the heritage and cultural significance of Carnival.”

Rooted in communities

Vincent Madden, director of Metropolitan Pub Company, added: “We believe that great pubs are rooted in the communities they serve. These events are an opportunity to celebrate the history and cultural richness of West London while supporting an important community organisation.” Notting Hill Carnival first began as a response to racial tension and violence in London, including the 1958 Notting Hill race riots and the racist murder of Antiguan man Kelso Cochrane. Trinidadian activist and newspaper editor Claudia Jones, now known as the 'Mother of Notting Hill Carnival', organised an indoor Caribbean Carnival at St Pancras Town Hall in Camden in January 1959 to help improve relations in the area. The televised indoor event featured steel bands, calypso music, and dancing to boost morale and showcase West Indian culture. By 1966 the event had moved outdoors as the brainchild of social worker Rhaune Laslett, who persuaded a local steel band to travel through the streets playing steel pan music. As the troupe progressed along Portobello Road, local residents gathered to dance, transforming the occasion into a celebration, and marking the start of what we today know as Carnival. Notting Hill Carnival takes place this year from Saturday 29 August to Monday 31 August 31, and the Metropolitan Pub Company events line-up includes: The Prince Bonaparte, Westbourne Park – 4 August Carnival is 60. What Next? will bring together Ansel Wong CBE and guest speakers for a panel discussion exploring the future of Carnival over the next 60 years and will also feature live poetry readings and calypso music. The Mitre, Holland Park – 11 August Guests will take part in a guided tasting of Bumbu, the Barbadian rum brand, discovering its history and Caribbean roots through a curated tasting experience. The Ladbroke Arms, Notting Hill – 25 August A 90-minute guided walking tour led by Yvette Reinfor will explore hidden local histories and celebrate the Caribbean community that played a key role in shaping Notting Hill Carnival. The walk ends at The Ladbroke Arms with a fish and chip taster and a half pint of the pub's House Ale.

Big boost

As the drinks business reported, Carnival can offer a big boost for drinks brands with research group Williams determining that domestic visitors spend an estimated £58.5 million on food and drinks alone during Notting Hill Carnival, while international visitors add £20.3m to this. Rum brand Duppy Share told db that it sold more than 2,000 bottles of rum and 4,000 canned cocktails over four days at the 2024 Notting Hill Carnival. Not only can the event increase the visibility of brands, it also offers the chance to offer collectible versions of favourite drinks linked to Carnival. Last year, Hennessy debuted its own float at Notting Hill Carnival alongside a limited-edition bottle of Hennessy V.S, swapping the label’s traditional gold scrollwork for a bold feather motif inspired by Carnival colours and energy.

title: Exploring eight EU wine regions set to win over drinkers
summary:
The EU is at the heart of the international wine trade, with its position built on quality assurance and regulation. A recent masterclass explored how that is driving innovation in its emerging regions.

The post Exploring eight EU wine regions set to win over drinkers appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
The EU is at the heart of the international wine trade, with its position built on quality assurance and regulation. A recent masterclass explored how that is driving innovation in its emerging regions. Those working in the UK wine trade will be used to tastings highlighting a single winery’s portfolio. They may have attended masterclasses surveying a producers association, a popular grape variety or, perhaps, a wider region. A recent masterclass in Cardiff, however, took a grander view. Although it surveyed a number of wines through the lenses of variety and region, its theme was significantly larger: the strength of the entire EU as a wine-producing bloc. In that endeavour, Neil McAndrew served as guide. During 35 years in the wine trade, he has worked across retail, distribution and fine wine, in addition to a current role advising the EU’s ‘More Than Only Food & Drink’ campaign. Over that time he has – quite literally – seen the EU grow, with new nations joining, bringing indigenous varieties and traditional winemaking. He believes the EU’s wine scene is stronger than ever. “There’s no doubt that the EU is in a fantastic position in terms of the breadth of producers, styles of wine and grape varieties,” he commented. “It is absolutely the epicentre of wine production in the world.” That is more than just a statement of Europe’s size. Although geographical spread is important, just as vital is the structure under which EU wine is produced. According to the European Parliament’s 2023 briefing on the EU wine sector, 65% of wine in the EU is made under a Protected Designation of Origin (PDO). This means that production, processing and preparation must take place within a specific geographical area, and under stipulated guidelines to match the regional style. A further 17% falls under a Protected Geographical Indication (PGI), meaning that at least one of those processes must take place in the geographical area. The EU also has its own certification for organic production. These programmes matter because they underpin the EU’s unique offering. Across its wines – indeed, across its other food and drink products – they contribute three pillars that offer the consumer confidence: authenticity, sustainability and quality.

What marks out EU wine?

The PDO and PGI schemes mean that consumers can trust what is in the bottle. On a very basic level, that means assurances of product safety and traceable origin. Yet more and more, consumers are recognising the schemes as custodians of heritage, and promoters of forward-thinking winemaking When it comes to authenticity, the EU has a significant advantage over other wine-producing regions. With the PDO and PGI systems to promote regional specialities, its producers have ample opportunities to lean into their local identity. As Europe is the home of Vitis vinifera, the bloc has a huge wealth of native grapes to showcase. By prioritising those varieties, as well as distinctive terroirs and Europe’s remarkable stock of old vines, the EU has a strong trajectory that does not rely on replicating the same styles in every region. PDOs and PGIs protect local traditions and mean that consumers come to recognise their distinctiveness and seek out such wines. In fact, McAndrew identified a number of emerging consumer trends that will benefit EU producers in coming years: island wines with unique terroirs, Central European nations with indigenous grapes, and expertise with hybrid grapes to protect against climate change. As more UK businesses get wise to the diversity of EU production, especially in the on-trade and in the speciality off-trade, these trends represent a key commercial opportunity. Sustainability has proved a further advantage for EU producers. Through its schemes – notably the EU’s organic certification, but also through some PDOs and PGIs mandating sustainable production – the EU is making sure that consumers have highly sustainable options when buying wine. The organic certification, for instance, limits the use of pesticides and promotes animal welfare in production. Organic wines now make commercial sense, as well as ethical sense, McAndrew explained. “The category is expected to grow 10% every year to 2030, and that’s quite significant, given where we’re coming from,” he said. “A lot of organic wine comes from France, Spain and Italy, but Greece, Bulgaria and Romania are all in the top 20 organic wine regions in the world.” (Citing data sourced from FiBL and IFOAM’s The World of Organic Agriculture 2026.) As for quality, that was on show in the second part of McAndrew’s masterclass. Taking eight wines from across the EU as his starting point, he demonstrated how those principles translate from an EU-wide structure to great wines from exciting origins.

Landwein der Saar PGI, Germany

McAndrew began with this PGI, which presented one of Europe’s most recognisable grape varieties in an unexpected context. The example he chose was a Sekt made with Riesling grown in the Saar’s steep slate vineyards, demonstrating this grape variety’s potential in traditional method sparkling winemaking. Sourced from vines that are more than 100 years old, the wine showed the concentration possible from long-lived vineyards, while 12 months of lees ageing contributed a creamy mousse. Elegant, mineral and bone-dry, it lived up to the region’s characteristic intensity without being too heavy.

Κρασοχωρια Λεμεσου PDO, Cyprus

This Cypriot PDO (also known as the Wine Villages of Limassol), which spans high-altitude sites, allows a number of grape varieties, but the local Xynisteri is a standout. The white grape now accounts for 23% of the country’s vineyards (according to ampelographic tome Wine Grapes). Although historically associated with Commandaria dessert wine, elegant dry white examples are increasingly gaining ground. McAndrew presented one such wine, which showed off its citrus and spice notes, as well as a broad texture from maturation on the lees. The wine was also certified organic, a further tick for customers looking to drink authentic wines that protect their historic landscapes.

Tokaj PDO, Hungary

The PDO wines of Tokaj (or Tokaji, depending on your preference) need little introduction among wine lovers; decadently sweet botrytised examples have firmly placed them in the fine wine pantheon. Yet the area’s dry wines, particularly those based on Furmint (as was shown in the masterclass) prove the value of indigenous grape varieties. With characteristic acidity and vineyards on volcanic soils, the wines typically have freshness and energy. This allows for versatility: the acidity can be embraced with a zesty fruit profile, or played against waxiness and a touch of residual sugar for added weight.

Πλαγιεσ Αιγιαλειασ PGI, Greece

In the northern Peloponnese, you can find a fantastic combination of high-altitude sites (sometimes more than 1,000 metres above sea level) and coastal breezes. This PGI, also known as Slopes of Aigialeia, makes full use of those freshening influences. The PGI regulations allow producers some choice in grape varieties, but in Cardiff an unusual local speciality was given the spotlight. McAndrew presented a wine made with Lagorthi, a weighty, lightly aromatic variety, that had been vinified with fermentation on the skins and some clay amphorae ageing for added texture.

Murfatlar PDO, Romania

“Wines like this are the future,” McAndrew enthused, as he introduced a Fetească Neagră from the Romanian PDO. The region certainly has much to commend it: in sunny vineyards near the Black Sea, it creates intense, concentrated wines. Fetească Neagră, meanwhile, is drought- and cold-resistant, providing growers with reassurance in changing climatic conditions. The example shown was treated as many international fine red wines are, with careful oak ageing to integrate flavours and foster velvety tannins. The estate is the first to gain biodynamic certification in Romania, a further selling point.

Stredoslovenská PDO, Slovakia

Also known as Stredoslovenský or Stredoslovenské, this Slovakian region was the northernmost on display at the masterclass. The grape variety Frankovka is a true Central European speciality, and may be known to consumers as Austria’s Blaufränkisch. Although consumers may consider it an emerging region for wine, the volcanic hills have a viticultural heritage dating back to Roman times. McAndrew selected a bottle that fully embraced the bright cherry fruit, peppery spice and crunchy quality of the grape variety. With eight months spent in oak, it can offer an alternative to Chianti for the interested consumer.

Мелник PDO, Bulgaria

Situated in the valley of the Struma River in Bulgaria’s southwest, Мелник PDO (also known as Melnik PDO), enjoys a Mediterranean climate and vineyards combining sand and limestone. It is named after its grapes: there are, in fact, two Melnik varieties, one of which ripens early and the other late. The local varieties, which have long histories in the region, lend themselves to serious winemaking, as McAndrew’s audience discovered in a low-intervention, biodynamic example based on the early-ripening variety. He compared it to Syrah and Nebbiolo, particularly with 15 months in new French and Bulgarian barriques lending polish to the wine.

Utiel-Requena PDO, Spain

Just as the session began with an unexpected wine from a well-known wine-producing nation, so did it close. Utiel-Requena PDO proves that Spain has more to offer than Tempranillo; the Valencian region has made local variety Bobal its calling card. Among its chief assets is a wealth of old vines, lending concentration and tannic richness. Its bold, flavourful reds further benefit from a high-altitude plateau, contributing generous, ripe flavours, while the dry climate reduces disease pressure and means organic viticulture is common, as in the wine that McAndrew presented.

title: Lewis bets on Guinness and RTDs in Diageo recovery strategy
summary:
Sir Dave Lewis is going deep with cost cutting at Diageo, but he is also intent on restructuring the business to unlock greater value from its portfolio, writes Ron Emler.

The post Lewis bets on Guinness and RTDs in Diageo recovery strategy appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Sir Dave Lewis is going deep with cost cutting at Diageo, but he is also intent on restructuring the business to unlock greater value from its portfolio, writes Ron Emler.

Lewis said the company would continue to focus on premiumisation. “It's done very well for us,” he says, but his recovery plan also envisages some price adjustments. That, however, is only part of what he sees as being “competitive and returning to a norm”. “I'm talking about brand strength, quality of brand mixers, innovation.  Some of the pricing through Covid has got a little bit out of whack, and and we've adjusted some of those things."

'Drastic' Dave?

Lewis hates the nickname “Drastic” (earned from his days at Unilever and Tesco) and despite overseeing a swathe of job losses as duplicated roles are eliminated across the business, he is intent on developing the entire portfolio. “We are not hawking any of our brands”, he says, but vows to make them all work for shareholders. “We intend to activate a portfolio, so that we can serve more customers on more occasions.” Far from selling off Guinness, as some have speculated, a US$1 billion investment to double Guinness production capacity over the next five years is central to his plans, as he takes it deeper into global markets. The future for Guinness [which now makes up about 12% of group sales] is “very bright”.

Betting on RTDs

He wants to make up lost ground in the RTD market. Having once held almost a quarter of that sector Diageo now has about 10%. “We’re just going to roll up our sleeves and get on with our own business,” he says. He is especially critical of Diageo’s whiskey offerings in the RTD market. “We have not put our best foot forward in whiskey RTDs; I’m disappointed with the flavours”, he says, referring largely to Crown Royal. Change has already started with a US$20 million investment in a plant in the US, much of which will be devoted to expanding Crown Royal's presence in the fast-growing market for smaller pack formats while broadening its flavour range.

Premium pre-mixed

Lewis also argued that if around half of Scotch and other whiskies are consumed in mixed drinks, there is a significant opportunity to offer more premium ready-to-drink whisky serves. The US market is critical to Diageo, accounting for more than 35% of its global sales. Turning it around is the responsibility of new head John O’Keefe, who acknowledges that the group has seen “share declines across around 65% of our business” in America. He identifies Crown Royal, Smirnoff, Captain Morgan and Don Julio as the brands requiring the greatest attention, with poor packaging, weak marketing execution and non-availability of the right smaller pack sizes as key to their woes.

Restructuring for US growth

Lewis is backing him to put that right but knows that it will take at least two years to bring Diageo’s US market back to growth, even though O’Keefe is restructuring the business model. "We are moving from separate Spirits and Beer divisions to a single commercial organisation, with one commercial leader, one set of support functions and one set of key accounts. That is going to improve our agility immensely,” O’Keefe says. And notably Lewis points out that not one of O’Keefe’s plans for the US market involves crude price cuts. “There have been some weaknesses in our core brands for a number of years that have been covered up [by the growth of tequila]. That’s why we have lost share in North America. “These are very big, important brands which frankly we have not done a great job with. We need to go back and do that and also to recover the momentum with tequila. “We are confident we know how to do that, but it won’t be overnight”, says Lewis.
